title: Why "a leading provider of solutions" is meaningless marketing, and how to write specific messaging instead
summary: Jason Cohen attacks generic marketing language ("a leading provider of...", "solutions") using real company descriptions as examples. He argues the causes are fear, laziness, and incompetence, and that if you can't say what you do in a few specific words, customers won't get it either.

principles.text: Say plainly what you do, then spend your words on how you differ from competitors.
principles.quote: Turns out they do web analytics.  Oh.  They could have just said so and spent the rest of their words telling you how they're different from other web analytics companies.

principles.text: Filler phrases like "a leading provider of" carry no meaning; at best readers gloss over them, at worst they leave.
principles.quote: At best you gloss over it--an overused phrase, devoid of meaning.  At worst you lose interest and click the "Back" button.

principles.text: Startups can't afford bland, wishy-washy copy; generic phrasing is a big-company luxury born of fear.
principles.quote: This excuse might work at Big Company Inc, but in a startup you can't afford to be bland and wishy-washy.

principles.text: Nailing your message is hard work: know your customer, boil the company to its essentials, be succinct and specific.
principles.quote: You have to know your customer, boil your company down to its essentials, and be succinct and evocative and specific.  It's easier not to.

principles.text: Vague messaging often signals you don't know your differentiator, your niche, or your ideal customer.
principles.quote: What if you don't actually know what sets your product apart?  What if you can't articulate the niche your company owns?

principles.text: If you can't state your product in a few specific words, customers won't understand it either; cut every word that doesn't count.
principles.quote: If you can't articulate your product in a few, choice, specific, words, your potential customers won't get it either.
